lead: A pump is sold with a curve, not a single flow. At each flow Q the same pump gives a different head H, draws different power P and runs at different efficiency η. Plot these against Q and you get the performance curves. They exist because a pipe system also demands more head as flow rises. Where the pump curve meets the system curve is the duty point, the flow the pump will actually deliver. Every selection — a 1 hp domestic booster, a 50 kW irrigation set, a data-centre cooling pump — is a search for a safe duty point.
prereq: You need: 7.3 heads and efficiencies, 7.4 series and parallel, 7.5 NPSH, and see Unit 6, Specific speed and unit quantities, for the turbine analogy.

sections.h3: The four curves on one sheet

blocks.text: The main curve is head against flow, H(Q). It falls: a centrifugal impeller gives its highest head at zero flow, called shut-off head, and less head as flow rises toward the run-out end. The falling shape is why a fixed speed cannot fix both flow and head.

Efficiency η(Q) starts low, rises to a peak near the design flow, then falls. The peak is the best efficiency point, BEP. The rated point is the buyer's guarantee point, usually near BEP: a stated Q, H, η and shaft power P.
Shaft power P(Q) for a centrifugal pump usually rises with Q. At shut-off it is low but not zero, because disc friction and leakage remain. The motor must cover run-out power, not only duty power.
Required NPSH, NPSHR(Q), generally rises with Q. Available NPSH must stay above it, or cavitation occurs (see 7.5).

System head has two parts: static head H<sub>st</sub>, which is lift plus pressure difference and does not change with Q; and friction head, which grows roughly as Q². Write H<sub>sys</sub> = H<sub>st</sub> + kQ², where k is a constant for that pipe layout, in s²/m⁵ when Q is in m³/s and H in m.

Plot H<sub>sys</sub> on the same axes as pump head. The crossing satisfies H<sub>pump</sub>(Q) = H<sub>sys</sub>(Q). That Q and H are the duty point. It is the flow the pump can hold steadily with that pipe system.
A valve opening lowers k and moves the duty to higher Q. A valve closing raises k and moves it to lower Q. The rated point and the duty point can differ.

sections.h3: Specific speed and the affinity laws

blocks.where: N<sub>s</sub> is pump specific speed; N is shaft speed in rpm; Q is flow in m³/s at best efficiency; H is head in m at the same point.

blocks.text: N<sub>s</sub> is dimensional; it is not a dimensionless number. Low N<sub>s</sub> (often below 30) means a narrow radial-flow impeller. Medium values give mixed flow. High values (often above 80) give axial flow. The bands vary by maker, so use N<sub>s</sub> for selection, not as a strict law. Turbine specific speed in Unit 6 is a different definition; do not mix the two.

blocks.where: Q is flow, H is head, P is shaft power, and N is speed. The laws apply to the same pump and the same impeller diameter, while efficiency stays roughly unchanged.

blocks.text: A reciprocating pump traps a fixed volume each stroke. Its flow is almost constant and its head varies with load, so its H(Q) curve is nearly vertical. A centrifugal pump is the opposite: flow changes a lot while head falls. Reciprocating flow pulses; an air vessel smooths it (see 7.8). Slip is in 7.7.

figure.caption: Pump head falls while system head rises; the two lines cross at about 34.7 L/s and 24.3 m, the duty point for the worked example.

spec.aria: The falling pump-head curve meets the rising system-head curve at the duty point near 35 L/s and 24 m.

examples.question: A pump test at 1450 rpm gives head 40 m at 0 L/s, 38 m at 10 L/s, 34 m at 20 L/s, 28 m at 30 L/s and 20 m at 40 L/s. The system head is 12 m at 0 L/s, 13 m at 10 L/s, 16 m at 20 L/s, 21 m at 30 L/s and 28 m at 40 L/s. Plot both curves and estimate the duty flow and head.
steps: At each listed Q, find the difference H<sub>pump</sub> − H<sub>sys</sub>. At Q = 0 L/s: 40 − 12 = 28 m. At 10 L/s: 38 − 13 = 25 m. At 20 L/s: 34 − 16 = 18 m. At 30 L/s: 28 − 21 = 7 m. At 40 L/s: 20 − 28 = −8 m.
The difference changes sign between 30 L/s and 40 L/s, so the duty point lies between them.
Use linear interpolation between the two points. The drop over 10 L/s is 7 − (−8) = 15 m. The duty flow is Q<sub>d</sub> = 30 + 10 × (7 ÷ 15) = 34.67 L/s.

Find head on the pump curve between 30 L/s and 40 L/s. It falls by 8 m over 10 L/s, so H<sub>d</sub> = 28 − 8 × (4.67 ÷ 10) = 24.27 m. The system curve gives the same value: 21 + 7 × (4.67 ÷ 10) = 24.27 m.
Round to practical readings: duty flow ≈ 34.7 L/s, duty head ≈ 24.3 m.
examples.answer: The duty point is about 34.7 L/s at 24.3 m head.

traps: The duty point is where pump head equals system head, not the peak-efficiency point unless the system curve also passes there.
In N<sub>s</sub> use Q in m³/s, not L/s, and H in m; 35 L/s is 0.035 m³/s.
Affinity laws apply to the same pump and impeller diameter, not to two different pump models.
Shut-off head is at zero flow; it is not the rated head or the duty head.
A centrifugal pump's power usually rises with flow; do not size the motor from shut-off power alone.

quiz.q: Define shut-off head and run-out flow.
quiz.a: Shut-off head is pump head at Q = 0. Run-out is the high-flow end of the pump curve, beyond the rated point.

quiz.q: Why does a centrifugal pump's efficiency curve have a peak?
quiz.a: At low flow, recirculation and disc friction dominate; at high flow, hydraulic friction and shock losses rise. Between them, losses are least, so η peaks.

quiz.q: A pump at 1450 rpm gives 20 L/s. Estimate flow at 1740 rpm by the affinity law.
For N = 1450 rpm, Q = 0.035 m³/s, H = 24 m, find N<sub>s</sub>.
A pump runs at its peak-efficiency flow, but the system curve crosses the pump curve at a lower flow. Which is the duty point and why?
quiz.a: The lower-flow crossing is the duty point. Duty is fixed by H<sub>pump</sub> = H<sub>sys</sub>, not by peak efficiency.

quiz.q: What happens to duty flow when a discharge valve is partly closed?
quiz.a: k increases, the system curve steepens, and the intersection moves left: duty flow falls and head rises along the pump curve.
Q ∝ N, H ∝ N², P ∝ N³ for the same pump.
Its value changes with the units of N, Q and H; it is not a pure number.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, pump curves are stored as digital data and the duty point is found with a solver when the system has several branches. Variable-speed drives use the affinity laws to trim flow without a valve, saving energy. Search for 'pump selection software', 'variable speed pump curve', and 'best efficiency point'.
